accuracy.evidence: Checked against RSPB and British Antarctic Survey notes on Arctic tern migration (Arctic breeding, Antarctic summer; tracking studies about 70,000–90,000 km a year), US FWS / WWF accounts of the eastern North American monarch roost in oyamel fir forests of central Mexico and the multi-generation return, Serengeti–Mara wildebeest movement following rainfall and fresh grass, and NOAA Fisheries notes that humpbacks feed on krill and small fish in cold high-latitude waters then migrate to warmer waters to calve and feed little there. Hibernation (hedgehog in its nest) is staying put, not a long trip. Parameterised counts: p3 a+b migrants; p4 two one-way flights a year so 2n; m5 answer a; m6 t+w. Every lab match (tern/poles, monarch/Mexico, wildebeest/Serengeti, whale/cold-to-warm) agrees with those sources.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented slips for this topic: treating a one-way move as migration (the tern 'finds a new home'); thinking the animal gets lost; mixing routes (monarch or wildebeest as pole-to-pole); thinking humpbacks swim to the tropics to feed on krill; calling hibernation migration because both happen in winter; thinking any small daily movement (a snail) counts. Each appears as a prediction option, a pickWhy/pickWhale/dropRoute/drop message, or a challenge tag (oneway, hibernate, food, mix).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagmigrate is built around a round-trip map: the child flies a tern from the north cap to the south cap and back, then drops four animals onto four different routes and matches each reason (grass after rain, calves in warm water, winter in Mexico, summer food pole to pole). A later step isolates the whale feeding-vs-calving trap, and a sort separates migration from staying or hibernating. flaganwhere and flaghome place animals in habitats or shelters and never ask whether the animal returns. The lab cannot be reused for those topics by changing labels.

lab_teaches.evidence: Flying south alone is not enough: the first landing says 'Migration is not over: it will fly back,' and only the return marks the task complete, so the child discovers that a migration is a round trip. Wrong route drops name the animal that does belong there. The whale step prints 'Cold sea: food (krill)' and 'Warm sea: calves' on the canvas before the child picks, so the text confirms what they have just seen. The hedgehog's wrong-bin message names hibernation.

predictions.evidence: Five predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab then disproves: the tern 'finds a new home' or 'gets lost'; the longest pole-to-pole flight is the monarch or the wildebeest; wildebeest travel 'to fly to Mexico' or 'sleep in a nest'; whales swim to warm seas 'to feed on more krill' or 'roost in trees'; and a hedgehog in its winter nest is migrating 'because it is away for the season'. reveal() names their pick and the right answer.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven rotating questions (definition, longest migrant, whale reason, wildebeest grass, hibernation, monarch Mexico, snail). Each wrong choice has its own tag and message: oneway (leaving for good is not migration), hibernate (staying in a nest is not a long trip), food (krill is in the cold sea), mix (do not swap tern, monarch, whale and wildebeest). Answer order rotates each turn.

readability.evidence: Kid explanation FK combined 4.6 (family limit 5.0), adult combined 5.5 (limit 10.0). The curriculum words migration, hibernation, breeding, seasons, pole to pole, Serengeti and calves are each used with their meaning. Kid sentences stay short; adult paragraph 1 was split so a long curriculum sentence did not sit at grade 13.

no_filler.evidence: Each kid paragraph teaches one idea (a round trip for a reason; tern and monarch routes; wildebeest grass and whale calves; staying put and hibernation). The word journey, which the filler gate bans, was never used: the lesson says trip, travel, fly, swim and migration instead. The adult text gives sources, four named mistakes and what each lab step does.

mobile.evidence: The schematic Earth is an ellipse sized with rx=min(W×0.42, 170), so it fits at 390 px with N and S labels. Route spots are 18 px radius tap targets with short labels ('to Mexico', 'Serengeti'). Sort bins are half-width at the bottom. Every action has a button with min-height 48 px under the canvas, and feedback wraps to two lines.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button twin (Fly south / Fly back north, four route names, reason choices, Migrates / Stays nearby). Animals can be dragged into sort bins or the bins can be tapped; the map caps and route spots are also tappable. The canvas aria-label and live region update on every piece of feedback. Challenge answers sit in a labelled group with a polite live region. Fills use theme tokens mixed into C.pn so land, sea and ice keep contrast in both light and dark.

sources: National Curriculum in England: science programmes of study, KS1 Animals including humans and KS1/KS2 living things and their habitats; seasonal change (DfE, 2013)
RSPB and British Antarctic Survey: Arctic tern migration and geolocator tracking distances
US Fish and Wildlife Service and WWF: eastern North American monarch migration to central Mexico, multi-generation return
NOAA Fisheries: humpback whale feeding in high-latitude waters and migration to tropical calving grounds
Serengeti–Mara wildebeest migration: rainfall and grazing (Ngorongoro Conservation Area / TANAPA briefings; standard KS2 accounts)
